title: A day of truth
hookLine: no stretching, no shrinking: one day of words that match what happened
tomorrow: what keeps a decision standing once the feeling fades?

cards: I'm five minutes away, says someone still at home. That movie was literally the best thing ever. No worries, from someone who's worried.
Nobody counts these, which is the point: the little untruths are the ones that don't feel like lies. Today asks for an odd experiment. One day where what you say is exactly true.

teach.b: The precept is short: refrain from false speech. The path spells out right speech more fully, and in one discourse the Buddha describes his own speech as true, beneficial, and spoken at the right time.
Treat those as three checks, not one.
Exaggeration fails the first, quietly. It isn't exactly false, but it isn't what happened either. The white lie fails the first too, though it hopes to pass the second.
And a true thing blurted at the wrong moment fails the third. Here's something to tell a friend tonight.
In the talk with the dipper, the Buddha also asks Rahula about a mirror. What's a mirror for? For reflecting, sir.
In the same way, he says, reflect before you act, while you act, and after, and speaking is one of those acts.
So a day of exact speech is mostly a day of tiny pauses: is this true, is it helpful, is it time? Not a vow of silence. Just words that match the world they describe.

how: Right speech is part of the Buddha's eightfold path, and some Buddhists keep a day of careful speech, with no exaggeration or white lies, as a practice of the perfection of truthfulness.

games.q: what does “a day of truth” mean?
o: a day of saying every thought out loud
a day of speech exactly as true as what happened
a day of staying silent from morning to night

games.q: three checks and a mirror — tap the pairs.

s: exaggerating isn't really lying, so it doesn't count
it fails the first check: it isn't what happened.
the Buddha used a mirror to teach Rahula to reflect before acting
exact speech means saying every true thing you think
the Buddha also asks: is it beneficial, and is it the right time?

games.q: a coworker asks how your weekend was. it was fine, honestly a little boring. which answer is exactly true?
o: quiet, a bit boring, and that was fine.
amazing, honestly one of the best ones.
games.why: exact speech isn't gloomy or glowing. it matches what happened: no stretching, no shrinking.

practice: Open your messages and reread the last few things you sent. Find one line that was a little bigger, smaller or softer than what was true, and say the exact version quietly out loud.
No need to send anything; just hear how exact sounds.

wordCard.voice: A day of truth: one ordinary day of speech that is exactly true, checked like a mirror.

orig.note: Pali: right speech, one part of the path the Buddha taught.

carryVoice: For the road: exactly true, not bigger, smaller or softer than what actually happened. Until next time.

sources.ref: MN 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (speech that is true, beneficial and at the right time)
MN 61, Ambalatthika-Rahulovada Sutta (the mirror: reflect before, during and after acting by body, speech and mind)
